title: A Practical Guide to Cloud Migration for South African Organisations
excerpt: Cloud migration doesn't have to be risky. Here's a phased approach that keeps your organisation running while you modernise.

children.text: Moving to the cloud is one of the highest-impact decisions an organisation can make — but it is also where many projects stall. The difference between a smooth migration and a painful one usually comes down to preparation, not technology.
Start with an honest assessment
Before you move a single workload, map what you actually have. Catalogue your applications, the data they depend on, and how critical each one is to daily operations.
Which systems are business-critical versus nice-to-have?
What are the data residency and compliance requirements?
Which applications are cloud-ready, and which need work first?
Choose the right migration strategy
There is no single correct approach. Most organisations use a mix, chosen per workload rather than applied across the board.
Rehost, replatform or refactor
A quick
rehost
(“lift and shift”) gets you to the cloud fast. A
replatform
makes small optimisations along the way, while a
refactor
rebuilds an application to be cloud-native. Match the effort to the value.
Plan for security and compliance from day one
Security is not a phase you bolt on at the end. Identity, access control and backup should be designed in from the start. For South African organisations, the
Protection of Personal Information Act
shapes where and how personal data can be stored.
The safest migration is the one you can reverse. Always keep a tested rollback path until a workload is proven in production.
Measure, optimise, repeat
Once workloads are live, watch cost and performance closely. Cloud spend can creep quietly, so set budgets and alerts early, right-size resources, and revisit them every quarter.

seoDescription: A phased, low-risk approach to cloud migration for South African organisations — assessment, strategy, security and cost control.

title: Five Cybersecurity Habits Every SME Should Adopt in 2026
excerpt: You don't need an enterprise budget to be secure. These five habits stop the majority of common attacks.

children.text: Smaller organisations are targeted precisely because attackers assume their defences are weaker. The good news: a handful of consistent habits blocks the overwhelming majority of real-world attacks.
Turn on multi-factor authentication everywhere
Passwords leak. Multi-factor authentication (MFA) means a stolen password alone is not enough to get in. Enable it on email, banking and every admin account first.
Patch quickly and automatically
Most breaches exploit known vulnerabilities that already have fixes. Turn on automatic updates for operating systems and browsers, and keep an inventory so nothing is quietly left behind. Even
winget upgrade --all
on a schedule is better than nothing.
Back up — and test your restores
A backup you have never restored is a hope, not a plan. Follow the 3-2-1 rule and rehearse recovery so you know it works before you need it.
Three copies of your data,
on two different types of media,
with one copy kept off-site or in the cloud.
Train your people
Technology stops a lot, but people are the last line of defence. Short, regular phishing awareness sessions consistently outperform a single annual lecture.
Have a plan before you need one
Write down who to call, how to isolate affected systems, and how you will communicate during an incident. A one-page plan practised twice a year beats a detailed document nobody has read.
Security is not a product you buy once. It is a set of habits you keep.

seoDescription: Five practical cybersecurity habits that protect small and medium businesses from the most common attacks.

title: Getting the Most Out of Microsoft 365 for Hybrid Teams
excerpt: Most organisations use a fraction of what Microsoft 365 offers. Here's how to turn it into a real digital workplace.

children.text: Microsoft 365 is more than email and a word processor. Used well, it becomes the connective tissue of a hybrid workplace — but only if you go beyond the defaults.
Make Teams the front door
When Teams becomes the place work happens — chat, meetings, files and apps together — people stop hunting across a dozen tools. Structure it around how teams actually work, not your org chart.
Tame file sprawl with SharePoint
Shared drives quietly become a mess. SharePoint document libraries with clear ownership, versioning and metadata make information findable again.
One source of truth per team or project,
consistent naming and folder depth,
permissions reviewed on a regular cadence.
Automate the busywork with Power Platform
Approvals, notifications and simple data entry are perfect candidates for automation. Power Automate and Power Apps let you remove repetitive steps without a large development effort.
Govern access with Entra ID
Identity is the new perimeter. Use
Microsoft Entra ID
with conditional access and MFA so the right people reach the right resources — and no one else does.
Adoption beats features. A tool only helps once people genuinely use it every day.

title: Building a Resilient Network: LAN, WAN and Wi-Fi Best Practices
excerpt: Downtime is expensive. These fundamentals keep your network fast, secure and dependable as you grow.

children.text: A network is invisible until it fails — and then it is the only thing anyone talks about. Resilience is designed in, not added later.
Design for redundancy
Single points of failure are where outages begin. Dual internet links, redundant switches and failover paths keep you running when — not if — something breaks.
Segment your network
Flat networks let a problem in one place spread everywhere. Separating guests, staff, servers and devices limits the blast radius of any incident and makes traffic easier to reason about.
Keep guest Wi-Fi isolated from internal systems,
put servers and workstations on separate segments,
give operational devices their own controlled network.
Wi-Fi that actually works
Coverage is not the same as capacity. A proper site survey, sensible channel planning and enough access points make the difference between reliable Wi-Fi and constant complaints.
Monitor everything
You cannot fix what you cannot see. Continuous monitoring turns firefighting into prevention, catching failing hardware and saturated links before users notice.
The goal is boring: a network so dependable that nobody has to think about it.

seoDescription: LAN, WAN and Wi-Fi best practices for building a resilient, secure and dependable business network.

title: What IoT Means for Facilities and Operations Teams
excerpt: Connected devices are moving from buzzword to budget line. Here's where they pay off — and what to watch out for.

children.text: The Internet of Things (IoT) has quietly become practical. For facilities and operations teams, it is less about hype and more about visibility — knowing what is happening across your sites in real time.
What IoT actually is
At its simplest, IoT means everyday equipment fitted with sensors that report back over the network. That data becomes the basis for automation and better decisions.
Where it pays off first
Start where measurement translates directly into savings or safety.
Energy and utilities monitoring to cut waste,
predictive maintenance that flags failures early,
environmental sensors for temperature-sensitive areas,
occupancy data to right-size space and cleaning.
Don't forget security
Every connected device is a potential entry point. Keep IoT devices on a segmented network, change default credentials, and apply firmware updates like you would any other system.
Getting started
Begin with one measurable problem, prove the value, then expand. A small, well-scoped pilot teaches you more than a sweeping rollout — and builds the confidence to scale.
Collecting data is easy. The value comes from acting on it.
